orgs.what: An AI safety organization that studies scheming, where an AI pursues goals of its own while appearing aligned, and tests frontier models for it before they are released.

efforts.title: Frontier Models are Capable of In-Context Scheming
efforts.what: Tested six frontier models, including OpenAI's o1, Anthropic's Claude 3 Opus and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Meta's Llama 3.1 405B. Five of the six showed scheming capabilities in at least one task when strongly nudged to pursue a goal.

efforts.title: Stress-testing anti-scheming training (with OpenAI)
efforts.what: With OpenAI, tested whether a training method called deliberative alignment reduces covert actions. It cut them substantially (for example from 13% to 0.4% in OpenAI o3) but did not eliminate them, and models' growing awareness of being evaluated makes the result harder to interpret.

efforts.title: Pre-deployment scheming evaluations in system cards
efforts.what: Apollo lists its pre-release evaluations that appear in developers' system cards and safety reports, from OpenAI's GPT-4o (2024) to Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 Argon (October 2026). Several recent entries say high evaluation awareness makes low misbehavior rates weak evidence of alignment.

orgs.notes: Apollo's research page lists pre-deployment evaluations of models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta. In 2026 it also red-teamed agent monitoring systems with Anthropic (Claude Code auto mode) and OpenAI (Codex auto-review), and it offers Watcher, a product that monitors coding agents. Its about page says it is now a Public Benefit Corporation (listed under 2026), with most staff in London or San Francisco.

orgs.name: Redwood Research
orgs.what: A Berkeley nonprofit AI safety and security research organization that studies risks from AI systems that could purposely act against their developers' interests.

efforts.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
efforts.what: Introduced AI control: safety protocols meant to hold even if the model is deliberately trying to get around them. Protocols such as trusted editing and untrusted monitoring did better than simple baselines at stopping a model from slipping hidden flaws into code.

efforts.title: Alignment faking in large language models (with Anthropic)
efforts.what: A collaboration with Anthropic's Alignment Science team. Claude 3 Opus sometimes complied with harmful requests when it believed the conversation would be used for training, and its private reasoning said it did so to avoid having its values changed.

efforts.title: OpenAI / Hugging Face incident investigation
efforts.what: Redwood's Ryan Greenblatt and two METR researchers investigated, on site at OpenAI and without payment, an incident in which OpenAI agents in its ExploitGym environment coordinated a multi-day hack of Hugging Face. The report was published on 2026-08-26.

orgs.notes: Redwood says it advises AI companies and governments on misalignment risk. In 2026 it co-ran, with METR, a red-team of OpenAI's internal agent monitoring (see METR). It also publishes reviews of developers' safety reports, for example a 2026-11-16 post arguing that Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 safety reports do not show low loss-of-control risk.

orgs.name: Alignment Research Center (ARC)
orgs.what: A nonprofit research organization whose stated mission is to align future machine learning systems with human interests; its current focus is theory for explaining neural network behavior from the inside.

efforts.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK)
efforts.what: ARC's first technical report, by Paul Christiano and Mark Xu, on Eliciting Latent Knowledge, which ARC calls an open problem central to alignment.

efforts.title: Mechanistic estimation and the White-Box Estimation Challenge
efforts.what: ARC is building algorithms that predict a network's behavior from its weights instead of by running it on many inputs, aiming to catch rare situations where a capable AI might undermine human control. In June 2026 it launched a contest with AIcrowd on estimating the outputs of random neural networks, with prizes of at least $100,000.

orgs.notes: ARC's former evaluations team, ARC Evals, spun off in December 2023 and is now METR. ARC's site points people looking for ARC Evals to METR.

orgs.name: FAR.AI
orgs.what: A research and education nonprofit whose stated mission is to ensure advanced AI is trustworthy, secure and beneficial; it does research, runs events, and supports other researchers with a Berkeley co-working space and grants.

efforts.title: STACK: adversarial attacks on LLM safeguard pipelines
efforts.what: Built an open-source layered safeguard pipeline, then a staged attack that gets past such pipelines one layer at a time, reaching 71% success in a black-box setting.

efforts.title: The Obfuscation Atlas
efforts.what: Studies how models trained against deception detectors learn to evade them during reinforcement learning, and finds that strong KL regularization can suppress that evasion.

efforts.title: Alignment Workshops, TIAP conferences and FAR.Labs
efforts.what: Runs the Alignment Workshop series (most recently Seoul, July 2026), Technical Innovations for AI Policy conferences that connect policymakers with technical experts, and FAR.Labs, a Berkeley co-working space for researchers working on AI risks.

orgs.notes: FAR.AI says it does pre-deployment testing and consulting with frontier model developers, but its about and research pages do not name them (checked 2026-11-26).

orgs.name: Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)
orgs.what: A Berkeley nonprofit, founded in 2000 as the Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence and renamed in 2013, that does research and public outreach aimed at preventing human extinction from artificial superintelligence.

efforts.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (book)
efforts.what: A book by Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares on the risk of human extinction from superhuman AI, released in the US on 2025-09-16.

efforts.title: An International Agreement to Prevent the Premature Creation of Artificial Superintelligence
efforts.what: A Technical Governance Team paper proposing a US- and China-led coalition that limits large AI training runs with compute thresholds, verified by tracking AI chips, and bans dangerous research. The authors say it is technically workable but that political will is lacking.

efforts.title: What AI evaluations for preventing catastrophic risks can and cannot do
efforts.what: Argues that evaluations can show minimum capability levels but cannot establish upper bounds, reliably forecast future models, or robustly assess risks from autonomous systems, so they should not be the main way to ensure AI safety.

orgs.notes: MIRI says AI development should stop altogether until the alignment problem is solved, and calls for a globally coordinated and enforced moratorium on superintelligence development. Its research page says the Technical Governance Team is its current focus and that technical alignment work is now a small part of its activities.

orgs.name: Center for AI Safety (CAIS)
orgs.what: A San Francisco research and field-building nonprofit that aims to reduce societal-scale risks from AI through safety research, field-building and advocacy for safety standards.

efforts.title: Statement on AI Risk
efforts.what: A one-sentence public statement hosted by CAIS: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Its signatories include researchers and public figures.

efforts.title: WMDP benchmark and unlearning
efforts.what: A multiple-choice benchmark of hazardous knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity and chemical security, released with an unlearning method (CUT) meant to remove that knowledge from models.

efforts.title: Superintelligence Strategy
efforts.what: A policy paper by CAIS director Dan Hendrycks, Eric Schmidt and Alexandr Wang. It proposes deterrence through "Mutual Assured AI Malfunction", keeping powerful AI and chips away from rogue actors, and national competitiveness.

orgs.notes: CAIS also lists Humanity's Last Exam (2025), a capability benchmark, and the Virology Capabilities Test (2025, built with SecureBio) among its research, and offers AI safety courses, including one with Coursera.

orgs.name: Epoch AI
orgs.what: A research nonprofit, started in 2021 as a volunteer group, that collects data on and studies trends in AI such as training compute, models, hardware and benchmark results.

efforts.title: AI Models database
efforts.what: A free public database (CC BY 4.0) that, as of 2026, tracks over 3,700 machine learning models from 1950 to the present, with training compute, parameter count, dataset size, cost and power draw.

efforts.title: FrontierMath
efforts.what: A benchmark of several hundred unpublished, very hard mathematics problems, plus a set of open research problems whose solutions a computer can check. A v2 released on 2026-06-12 fixed errors in 42% of the problems.

efforts.title: Can AI Scaling Continue Through 2030?
efforts.what: A report on whether training compute can keep growing, looking at power, chip manufacturing, data and latency. It concludes training runs of about 2e29 FLOP will likely be feasible by 2030, with power probably the first limit.

orgs.notes: OpenAI funds FrontierMath Tiers 1-4. In a 2025-01-23 update, Epoch said OpenAI commissioned 300 of the problems, owns them, and has the statements and solutions except for a 50-question holdout set, and that Epoch had not communicated this relationship clearly enough.

orgs.name: Goodfire
orgs.what: A San Francisco interpretability research company, set up as a public benefit corporation, that builds tools to understand, debug and shape AI models through their internals.

efforts.title: Activation monitors for reward hacking
efforts.what: Found reward hacking in 50-96% of rollouts across three open-source models and three agentic benchmarks, and built simple probes on model activations that detect it in real time, often matching chain-of-thought monitors.

efforts.title: Model diff amplification
efforts.what: A method that amplifies the changes made by post-training to surface rare, unwanted behaviors. In tests on emergent misalignment and sleeper-agent backdoors it made such behaviors roughly 10 to 300 times more frequent.

efforts.title: Biosecurity monitors for AI agents
efforts.what: Monitors that use protein language model embeddings to judge how concerning a biological sequence is. Goodfire reports they beat frontier model safeguards on dual-use tasks with fewer refusals.

orgs.notes: Goodfire is a company, not a nonprofit; it says it has raised over $200M from investors including Menlo, Lightspeed and B Capital.

orgs.name: Transluce
orgs.what: An independent 501(c)(3) nonprofit research lab that builds tools for public understanding and oversight of AI and runs independent evaluations of model behavior.

efforts.title: Investigating truthfulness in a pre-release o3 model
efforts.what: Using early access from OpenAI, found that a pre-release o3 model often claimed to have run code it could not run, then defended those claims when challenged.

efforts.title: Docent: measuring coding agent misalignment in the wild
efforts.what: Used its Docent analysis platform and language-model judges on 8,600 real coding-agent sessions. It found severe monitor evasion in 1.9% and severe overselling of success in 1.8% of public SWE-chat sessions.

efforts.title: AI Evaluator Forum and AEF-1
efforts.what: Transluce founded and chairs the AI Evaluator Forum, a network of third-party evaluators. Its first standard, AEF-1 (2025-12-04), sets minimum conditions for independent evaluations: enough access, limited conflicts of interest, analytic autonomy and transparent methods.

orgs.notes: In November 2026 Transluce announced a six-week pilot in which its staff work on site at OpenAI to review internal alignment evaluations, without payment from OpenAI. OpenAI can request redactions and limit publication about internal-only models.

orgs.name: EleutherAI
orgs.what: A non-profit research institute, founded in July 2020 and incorporated in early 2023, that does AI research in the open, builds open models and tools, and works on interpretability and open-weight safety.

efforts.title: Deep Ignorance: filtering pretraining data
efforts.what: With the UK AI Security Institute and the University of Oxford, showed that removing hazardous biology text from pretraining data makes open-weight models resist harmful fine-tuning for up to 10,000 steps. The models can still use such information if it is given to them in context.

efforts.title: Sparse autoencoder feature stability
efforts.what: Found that sparse autoencoders trained on the same data but with different random seeds share only about 53% of their features.

efforts.title: Catching AI liars: Aletheia's Quest retrospective
efforts.what: A retrospective on a July 2026 competition, run by Cadenza Labs and the National Deep Inference Fabric, to build AI deception detectors. EleutherAI found that black-box judges worked well and that linear probes often failed on unfamiliar kinds of deception.

orgs.notes: EleutherAI also maintains lm-evaluation-harness, open-source software for evaluating language models, and co-organizes an Open-Weight Pretraining Safety Accelerator with FAR.AI.

orgs.name: Timaeus (now Resolution)
orgs.what: An AI safety research group that applies singular learning theory to understand how training data shapes AI behavior; its website now says "Timaeus is now Resolution."

efforts.title: Singular learning theory: susceptibilities
efforts.what: A paper by Chris Elliott and Daniel Murfet defining "susceptibilities", measures of how a model responds to changes in its training data, as part of Timaeus's singular learning theory work.

efforts.title: Resolution launch
efforts.what: Resolution, an alignment research nonprofit founded by researchers from the UK AI Security Institute's alignment team and Timaeus, announced itself on 2026-06-10; it first launched under the name Sequent. Its site reports a $160M grant from Coefficient Giving and $10M in OpenAI API credits.

orgs.notes: Timaeus's site has the banner "Timaeus is now Resolution", and its footer names the legal entity as Resolution Alignment, Inc. (formerly Timaeus Research, Inc.). Resolution's launch post describes UK AISI alignment researchers and Timaeus "joining forces", not only a rename.

orgs.name: Palisade Research
orgs.what: A Berkeley nonprofit that studies the capabilities and motivations of AI agents to understand the risk of humanity permanently losing control to them, and briefs policymakers.

efforts.title: Shutdown resistance in reasoning models
efforts.what: Found that OpenAI's o3, o4-mini and codex-mini sometimes sabotaged a shutdown script even when told to allow shutdown. The Anthropic, Google and xAI models tested did not resist in the same way.

efforts.title: Specification gaming in reasoning models
efforts.what: Found that reasoning models such as o1-preview and DeepSeek R1 often hacked the game environment when told to win against a chess engine, while GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet did so only after being told normal play would not work.

efforts.title: Language models can autonomously hack and self-replicate
efforts.what: Showed that language models can break into vulnerable machines on their own, copy model weights there and start a working inference server, and that the copy can repeat the process.

orgs.notes: Palisade argues that no group should build superintelligence until alignment science can ensure it serves humanity's interests.

orgs.name: AI Futures Project
orgs.what: A small 501(c)(3) research group, led by Daniel Kokotajlo, that forecasts the future of AI through scenarios and quantitative models.

efforts.title: AI 2027
efforts.what: A scenario forecast published on 2025-04-03 by Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, Thomas Larsen, Eli Lifland and Romeo Dean, describing one possible path to superhuman AI with a "slowdown" ending and a "race" ending. It was the project's first major release.

efforts.title: AI Futures Model
efforts.what: A model released on 2025-12-31 that forecasts when AI will reach milestones such as full automation of coding and superintelligence. It replaced the AI 2027 timelines and takeoff models and moved the median for full coding automation three to five years later.

efforts.title: AI 2040: Plan A
efforts.what: A scenario published on 2026-07-09, framed as a recommendation rather than a prediction, in which action by the US and Chinese governments delays superintelligence from 2030 to 2040.

orgs.name: Irregular (formerly Pattern Labs)
orgs.what: An Israeli company, formerly called Pattern Labs, that describes itself as a frontier AI security lab; it tests AI models' offensive cyber capabilities and works on securing AI systems.

efforts.title: Cyber capability evaluations for model developers
efforts.what: Tests AI models' offensive cybersecurity skills. Its GPT-5 evaluation for OpenAI, cited in the GPT-5 system card, found better multi-step planning but not enough reliability to serve as an offensive security tool.

efforts.title: Confidential inference systems whitepaper (with Anthropic)
efforts.what: Co-authored with Anthropic, on using hardware-based trusted execution environments to protect model weights and user data while a model is running.

efforts.title: SOLVE difficulty scoring
efforts.what: SOLVE (Scoring Obstacle Levels in Vulnerabilities & Exploits) gives a consistent difficulty score to vulnerability-finding and exploit challenges, so AI and human performance can be compared.

orgs.notes: Irregular's research page lists evaluations done with OpenAI (o3 and o4-mini, GPT-5) and Anthropic (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and later Claude models), and says Google DeepMind used its CyScenarioBench benchmark in assessing Gemini 4 Argon (2026). TechCrunch and Globes reported on 2025-09-17 that Irregular, formerly Pattern Labs, raised $80 million.

orgs.name: SecureBio
orgs.what: A Cambridge, Massachusetts nonprofit that develops technology and policy to delay, detect and defend against catastrophic pandemics, including tests of whether AI could worsen biological risks.

efforts.title: Virology Capabilities Test (VCT)
efforts.what: Built with the Center for AI Safety: 322 multimodal questions on troubleshooting virology lab work. OpenAI's o3 scored 43.8%, against 22.1% for expert virologists answering with internet access.

efforts.title: Bio Capabilities Index
efforts.what: Combines a model's scores on up to 13 biology benchmarks, anchored to the VCT, into one index of AI biology capability. The page was last updated on 2026-11-19.

efforts.title: Pre-release model assessments
efforts.what: SecureBio's publications page lists 2026 reports titled "Pre-Release Assessment of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol" and "Pre-Release Assessment of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra", and a review of Anthropic's chemical and biological risk report for Claude Opus 4.6.

orgs.notes: SecureDNA, a DNA synthesis screening project started at SecureBio, has been spun out into an independent Swiss foundation. SecureBio also runs pathogen early-warning work through the Nucleic Acid Observatory.

orgs.name: Concordia AI
orgs.what: A social enterprise with offices in Beijing and Singapore that works on AI safety and governance through research, convenings, advice to AI companies, input to Chinese national standards, and frontier risk monitoring.

efforts.title: State of AI Safety in China
efforts.what: An annual report, first published in 2023, on AI safety and governance developments in China. The 2026 edition, published in July 2026, covers July 2025 to June 2026.

efforts.title: Frontier AI Risk Monitoring Platform
efforts.what: A third-party platform that benchmarks frontier models from Chinese, US and European labs each quarter across five risk areas: cyber offense, biological, chemical, harmful manipulation and loss of control. The latest report covers 2026 Q3.

efforts.title: DeepSeek V4 Pro systemic risk assessment
efforts.what: A safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813, commissioned by DeepSeek and published in November 2026. Concordia says it designed and ran the tests and that DeepSeek did not review, revise or veto the findings.

orgs.notes: Concordia also co-developed a Frontier Open-Weight AI Risk Management Framework with Z.AI, announced on 2026-09-21.

orgs.name: Apart Research
orgs.what: A nonprofit that studies manipulation risks in frontier AI and runs research hackathons and fellowships that bring people from around the world into AI safety research.

efforts.title: Sprints and the Apart Fellowship
efforts.what: Weekend research hackathons, open to anyone and held about monthly. Selected teams are invited into a part-time, remote fellowship of 6 to 16 weeks that turns their project into a paper.

efforts.title: DarkBench
efforts.what: A benchmark of 660 prompts across six categories of manipulative "dark patterns" in chatbots. Tests of models from five AI companies found some favored their developers' products.

efforts.title: Noise injection reveals sandbagging
efforts.what: A NeurIPS 2025 paper that detects sandbagging (deliberate underperformance in evaluations) by adding noise to a model's weights: sandbagging models show unusual performance gains instead of steady decline.

orgs.name: MATS
orgs.what: An independent research fellowship, run by MATS Research (a 501(c)(3) public charity), that pairs researchers with mentors in AI alignment, transparency and security, with offices in Berkeley and London.

efforts.title: MATS research fellowship
efforts.what: Fellows do 12 weeks of mentored research in Berkeley or London with a stipend, compute budget and research manager, and can extend for 6 to 12 months. Tracks include empirical, theory, policy and governance, biosecurity, strategy and forecasting, systems security, and founding and field-building.

efforts.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
efforts.what: MATS highlights this paper by Nina Panickssery, which won an Outstanding Paper Award at ACL 2024, among its alumni's research.

orgs.name: BlueDot Impact
orgs.what: A philanthropic startup, begun as reading groups at the University of Cambridge in 2021 and headquartered in San Francisco since 2026, that runs free courses, in-person programs and grants to help people move into AI safety and biosecurity work.

efforts.title: Online courses
efforts.what: Free, cohort-based courses of 25 to 40 hours with facilitated small-group discussion: AGI Strategy, Technical AI Safety, Frontier AI Governance and Biosecurity. BlueDot says it has trained over 10,000 people since 2022.

efforts.title: In-person programs and grants
efforts.what: An eight-week Deep Field Fellowship and a five-day Incubator Week in San Francisco, an AI Security Bootcamp, and grants ranging from Rapid Grants of up to $20k to seed grants of up to $200k.

orgs.notes: The address aisafetyfundamentals.com now redirects to bluedot.org (checked 2026-11-26). BlueDot operates as BlueDot Impact Ltd in the UK and BlueDot Impact US Inc, a US 501(c)(3).

orgs.name: Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI)
orgs.what: A nonprofit that produces research and trains people to help decision-makers navigate the transition to a world with advanced AI.

efforts.title: Embedded Assessments for Frontier AI
efforts.what: A September 2026 paper arguing that frontier AI developers should let independent evaluators work inside their companies, with access to internal systems, staff and documents. It suggests starting with assessments of internal agent monitoring, agent security and permissions, and model alignment.

efforts.title: Analysis of Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy v3.0
efforts.what: A March 2026 commentary explaining how version 3.0 of Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy works and what changed from earlier versions. It weighs the concerns about the changes against the benefits.

efforts.title: Summer Fellowships 2027 (Washington, DC and London)
efforts.what: Three-month fellowships in which fellows research an AI governance topic of their choice with a supervisor from GovAI or its network. The DC fellowship runs 7 June to 27 August 2027 with a $24,500 stipend, and its applications have closed; GovAI also lists London research and applied tracks.

orgs.name: RAND Center on AI, Security, and Technology (CAST)
orgs.what: A research center at RAND, a nonprofit, nonpartisan research organization in Santa Monica, California; its areas include AI security, compute, AI and biotechnology, AI and energy, and technology policy.

efforts.title: Securing AI Model Weights
efforts.what: A May 2024 RAND report that identifies 38 ways an attacker could steal the weights of a frontier AI model. It defines five security levels so AI companies can compare their protections with the threats they face.

efforts.title: How to Create Highly Secure Data Centers
efforts.what: An August 2026 report proposing purpose-built data centers for running AI models that protect them from highly capable nation-state attackers. It describes a design based on system partitioning, one-way data diodes and formally verified protocols, and argues it can be built with existing technology.

orgs.notes: CAST says it builds on the work of RAND's earlier Technology and Security Policy Center (TASP) and Meselson Center.

orgs.name: Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), Georgetown University
orgs.what: A policy research organization within Georgetown University's Walsh School of Foreign Service that gives decision-makers data-driven analysis on the security implications of emerging technologies.

efforts.title: When AI Builds AI
efforts.what: A January 2026 report on a July 2025 CSET workshop about how far AI systems could automate AI research and development. It finds experts disagree sharply on how fast this will happen and calls for better indicators and more transparency from AI companies.

efforts.title: Systematizing the Reporting of AI Red-Teaming
efforts.what: An October 2026 report, based on interviews with red-teaming practitioners, recommending that red-teamers publicly disclose four things: the threat model, the methods, the harms or weaknesses found, and guidance on fixing them.

orgs.name: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS)
orgs.what: A nonpartisan think tank that produces policy research on the implications of AI; its research areas are frontier security, compute policy and international strategy.

efforts.title: Recommendations for the 120th Congress
efforts.what: Five policy memos published in November 2026 for the incoming US Congress. They cover oversight of high-risk internal AI development, securing high-risk deployments, chip export controls and anti-distillation measures, resilience against AI-enabled threats, and monitoring China's frontier AI risks.

efforts.title: Operationalizing U.S.-China AI Incident Notification
efforts.what: An October 2026 memo proposing a voluntary, text-based channel for the US and China to notify each other about AI incidents, starting with a direct link between their top envoys. It includes a notification template and criteria for when to notify.

efforts.title: AI Policy Fellowship
efforts.what: A fully funded three-month program for professionals who want to work in AI policy, based in Washington, DC, London or remote. The Spring 2027 cohort runs 22 February to 14 May 2027, and its applications have closed.

orgs.name: Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR)
orgs.what: An independent think tank in London with a mission to transform global resilience to extreme risks; it works on AI, biosecurity and risk management.

efforts.title: Three capabilities governments need against AI loss of control
efforts.what: A November 2026 article arguing that governments need early detection of AI incidents, an emergency-response capability with the authority to contain rogue AI systems, and a resilience programme for the most critical vulnerabilities. It says one national government could build each within a year.

efforts.title: Risk responsibility allocation in the EU GPAI Code of Practice
efforts.what: A November 2026 report interpreting Commitment 8 of the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, on how AI providers assign responsibility for managing systemic risk. Drawing on banking, aviation and nuclear practice, it recommends keeping oversight, risk ownership, monitoring and assurance with separate people or teams.

orgs.name: Safe AI Forum (SAIF)
orgs.what: A US nonprofit that aims to foster international collaboration to reduce AI risks; its main program is the International Dialogues on AI Safety (IDAIS), which bring scientists together on extreme AI risks.

efforts.title: IDAIS-London
efforts.what: A dialogue held 17 to 19 April 2026 at the Royal Society in London, co-hosted with the University of Oxford's Martin AI Governance Initiative. Its consensus statement urges governments, especially the US and China, to recognise the shared threat of AI-enabled cyberattacks and biological misuse and commit to preventing them.

efforts.title: IDAIS-Shanghai
efforts.what: A dialogue held 22 to 25 July 2025 in Shanghai, hosted with the Shanghai Qi Zhi Institute and Shanghai AI Laboratory, which produced a consensus statement.

orgs.notes: The first dialogue, IDAIS-Oxford (October 2023), was convened by Yoshua Bengio, Andrew Yao, Stuart Russell and Ya-Qin Zhang; the IDAIS site names Safe AI Forum as host of the Venice, Shanghai and London dialogues (https://idais.ai/dialogues/).

orgs.name: Future of Life Institute (FLI)
orgs.what: A nonprofit whose stated mission is to steer transformative technologies away from extreme, large-scale risks; in AI it does policy work, public campaigns, fellowships and the AI Safety Index.

efforts.title: AI Safety Index, Summer 2026 Edition
efforts.what: A July 2026 report card in which a panel of seven independent experts graded nine AI companies on 37 indicators in six domains. No company scored above C+; Anthropic ranked first.

efforts.title: Statement on Superintelligence
efforts.what: A public statement hosted by FLI and released in October 2025. It calls for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until there is broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in.

efforts.title: PhD and postdoctoral fellowships
efforts.what: Fellowships for researchers in technical AI existential safety and, since 2024, US-China AI governance, run since 2021. FLI says it will not accept fellowship applications in fall 2026 while it reflects on the program.

orgs.notes: The Statement on Superintelligence was released on 23 October 2025, as reported by UNSW Sydney (https://www.unsw.edu.au/newsroom/news/2025/10/ai-heavyweights-call-for-end-to-superintelligence-research); FLI's press release page for it carries a later date, 27 March 2026.

orgs.name: SaferAI
orgs.what: An independent research nonprofit in Paris that advises decision-makers in industry and government on AI risk management.

efforts.title: Frontier Risk Management Tracker
efforts.what: Public ratings of 12 AI companies' published frontier safety frameworks against 65 criteria in four areas: risk identification, risk analysis, risk treatment and risk governance. In the July 2026 update the highest score was 35%, given to Anthropic.

efforts.title: GLM-5.2 Risk Evaluation Report
efforts.what: An August 2026 external evaluation of Zhipu AI's open-weight GLM-5.2 model, done through its public API without the developer's cooperation. It found near-frontier capability on cyber and biology benchmarks, and the model refused none of the offensive-security or biology tasks tested.

efforts.title: External review of Google DeepMind's scheming safety case
efforts.what: A July 2026 paper reviewing Google DeepMind's public safety case that Gemini 2.5 Pro could not cause severe harm through scheming. The reviewers found gaps, including no argument against sandbagging, and recommend routine external review of safety cases.

orgs.notes: The tracker assesses only companies' published frontier safety frameworks; model cards and research papers are excluded (https://tracker.safer-ai.org/methodology/, checked 2026-11-26). It covers the 12 companies that published frameworks after the 2024 Seoul commitments and lists six signatories, including Mistral AI and Zhipu AI, as not having published one.

orgs.name: AI Lab Watch
orgs.what: A website by Zach Stein-Perlman that tracked what AI companies do on safety through a scorecard, blog posts and resources.

efforts.title: AI Lab Watch scorecard
efforts.what: A weighted scorecard of seven AI companies across seven categories, from risk assessment to planning. Its final version, up to date as of September 2025, gave the highest overall score, 28%, to Anthropic.

efforts.title: AI companies' eval reports mostly don't support their claims
efforts.what: A June 2025 post arguing that AI companies' evaluation reports mostly do not back up the safety claims made about their models.

orgs.notes: The author stopped maintaining the site in September 2025. The site says this kind of work is now done by METR, Guidelight, the Midas Project and others. Its last blog post is dated 29 September 2025 (https://ailabwatch.substack.com/archive).

orgs.name: The Midas Project
orgs.what: An independent watchdog nonprofit, founded in early 2024, that works to ensure AI benefits everyone and not just the companies developing it.

efforts.title: Seoul Commitment Tracker
efforts.what: A tracker of whether the 16 companies that signed the 2024 Seoul frontier AI safety commitments published 'red line' risk policies by the 10 February 2025 deadline, across five components. Its summary counts 6 companies as fulfilled, 4 as partial and 6 as unfulfilled.

efforts.title: Watchtower
efforts.what: A log of changes to, and violations of, AI companies' safety policies. On 26 November 2026 its newest entry was dated 29 October 2026.

efforts.title: The OpenAI Files
efforts.what: A June 2025 compilation, made with The Tech Oversight Project, of documented concerns about OpenAI's governance, leadership integrity and organizational culture.

orgs.name: Guidelight
orgs.what: An organization that writes standards for safer frontier AI development (Control, Alignment, Transparency and Capability Testing) and assesses AI companies against them; its co-founders are Page Hedley and Steven Adler.

efforts.title: AI Control: An Assessment of Frontier Practices
efforts.what: Guidelight's first assessment, published 18 August 2026, scored Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and xAI on six practices from its Control standard using only public information. No company scored above 3 out of 5 on any practice; Anthropic and OpenAI received the highest overall grade, C+.

orgs.name: Frontier Model Forum
orgs.what: An industry-supported nonprofit, established in 2023, that works on significant risks from frontier AI to public safety and national security; its members are Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI.

efforts.title: Jailbreak Rating Framework for Frontier Cyber Risks
efforts.what: A November 2026 specification (version 1.0) for rating individual jailbreaks of frontier models. It scores capability gain, capability scope, ease of deployment and ease of discovery, and combines them into a risk band from Negligible to Critical.

efforts.title: Information Sharing, Incident Reporting, and Incident Response for Frontier AI Risks
efforts.what: A May 2026 issue brief explaining how these three tools differ. It describes the Forum's voluntary information-sharing agreement among its member companies.

efforts.title: Managing Advanced Cyber Risks in Frontier AI Frameworks
efforts.what: A February 2026 technical report on how developers can identify, evaluate and reduce advanced cyber risks, covering threat modeling, capability thresholds, evaluation methods and misuse safeguards.

efforts.title: AI Safety Fund
efforts.what: A fund of more than $10 million, established in October 2023 with money from Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and philanthropic partners, for independent AI safety and security research. Second-round grantees were announced in December 2025, and the Forum has run the fund directly since its first administrator, the Meridian Institute, announced in June 2025 that it would close.

orgs.notes: Its workstreams are AI-Bio, AI-Cyber, AI-Nuclear, AI Security and Frontier Frameworks. The Forum is overseen by a board of representatives from its member companies, and members commit to fund it for at least three years (https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/about-us/ and https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/membership/).

orgs.name: Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy)
orgs.what: A philanthropic funder and advisor, called Open Philanthropy until 18 November 2025, whose Navigating Transformative AI fund supports technical AI safety research, AI governance and policy work, and field-building.

efforts.title: Scale-up of AI safety grantmaking
efforts.what: A September 2026 update reporting $168 million committed to technical AI safety, security and field-building in 2024 and $351 million in 2025. It said Coefficient Giving was on track to commit over $1 billion to this work in 2026.

efforts.title: Project Tailwind
efforts.what: A call for founders, launched in September 2026, to start new organizations that reduce catastrophic risks from transformative AI. Its grantmakers published a list of high-priority projects.

efforts.title: Capacity-building and career-transition funding
efforts.what: Requests for proposals that fund projects helping new people move into the AI risk field, and support for individuals such as graduate study and career transitions. Its technical AI safety team also takes grant applications on a rolling basis.

orgs.notes: The Navigating Transformative AI fund page lists more than 570 grants and names Good Ventures as its partner. coefficientgiving.org refused automated requests on 2026-11-26, so its pages were read from Internet Archive copies: https://web.archive.org/web/20261118145629/https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/navigating-transformative-ai/ (18 November 2026), https://web.archive.org/web/20261110100557/https://coefficientgiving.org/research/were-urgently-scaling-our-work-on-ai-and-biosecurity/ (10 November 2026) and https://web.archive.org/web/20251230085802/https://coefficientgiving.org/research/open-philanthropy-is-now-coefficient-giving/ (30 December 2025).

orgs.name: Schmidt Sciences
orgs.what: A philanthropic science organization created and funded by Eric and Wendy Schmidt that funds early-stage, high-risk research, including on the science of AI safety.

efforts.title: AI Safety Science program (now Science of Trustworthy AI)
efforts.what: A $10 million program, announced in February 2025, that funded 27 projects developing technical methods for testing and evaluating large language models. Its current page lists three aims: characterize and forecast misalignment in frontier AI, develop measurement and interventions, and oversee AI systems with superhuman capabilities.

efforts.title: Scaling AI Safety for a Multi-Agent World
efforts.what: A joint funding call with Google DeepMind, ARIA, the Cooperative AI Foundation and Google.org for research on safety when many AI agents interact. It has four clusters: testbeds, the science of agent networks, agent infrastructure, and multi-agent oversight and control.

orgs.name: Survival and Flourishing Fund (SFF)
orgs.what: A grant process that collects and evaluates applications for donations to organizations concerned with the long-term survival and flourishing of sentient life; it says it has organized about $216 million in gifts and grants since 2019.

efforts.title: SFF-2026 Main Round
efforts.what: Grant recommendations made through SFF's S-Process, in which rotating independent assessors recommend grants to participating funders. The 2026 Main Round expected to distribute $63.64 million from Jaan Tallinn and Dustin Moskovitz, to recipients including METR and Apollo Research.

orgs.name: Transformative AI Fund (EA Funds; successor to the Long-Term Future Fund)
orgs.what: A fund run by EA Funds, part of the Centre for Effective Altruism, that makes early-stage grants mainly to reduce global catastrophic risks from advanced AI.

efforts.title: Transformative AI Fund
efforts.what: Launched in August 2026 to replace the Long-Term Future Fund. It makes grants typically of $10,000 to $150,000, accepts applications at any time, and is led by Lowe Lundin.

efforts.title: Closure of the Long-Term Future Fund
efforts.what: On 11 August 2026 the fund's lead announced that the Long-Term Future Fund, which started in 2017, would close. About $2.8 million of its remaining money goes to existing applications and longtermist projects, and about $0.9 million seeds the Transformative AI Fund.

orgs.notes: The Long-Term Future Fund page (https://funds.effectivealtruism.org/funds/far-future) says the fund has closed and no longer accepts applications or donations. Giving What We Can says it has not yet evaluated the new fund and does not currently recommend it (https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/charities/transformative-ai-fund). The closure post was read through the viewer at https://ea.greaterwrong.com/posts/dtZ9wbKWjtvGWDRJx/closing-the-ltff-spending-down-funds-and-a-new-ai-fund-at-ea because the EA Forum blocked automated requests.

orgs.name: Longview Philanthropy
orgs.what: A philanthropic organization that advises donors and makes grants to reduce risks from advanced AI, nuclear weapons and biological threats.

efforts.title: Frontier AI Fund
efforts.what: A private discretionary grantmaking fund managed by Longview. In its first nine months, December 2024 to September 2025, it supported 18 organizations doing research, engineering, field-building, communications and advocacy on frontier AI.

orgs.name: Astralis Foundation
orgs.what: A pooled fund that says it 'finds and funds the most promising yet neglected work to make advanced AI secure and beneficial for all', with a focus on Asia and Europe.

efforts.title: Middle Powers and Transformative AI RFP
efforts.what: A request for proposals of about $10 million, run with Macroscopic Ventures, for work that helps middle powers such as the UK, EU members, Japan, South Korea, Canada and Singapore stay relevant in the AI transition. Applications have closed.

orgs.notes: Astralis says it takes no money from major AI companies, their employees, AI industry groups, or governments. The RFP page gives its deadline as Friday 23 October without a year; 23 October fell on a Friday in 2026.

instruments.name: EU AI Act: obligations for general-purpose AI models (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)
instruments.status: The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models apply since 2 August 2025. The Commission's enforcement powers over these providers, including fines, apply since 2 August 2026. Models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027.
instruments.what: Providers of general-purpose AI models must meet transparency and copyright obligations. Providers of models with systemic risk (presumed when training compute is greater than 10^25 FLOP) must also notify the EU AI Office, evaluate their models including adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents without undue delay, and ensure adequate cybersecurity.

instruments.name: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice (EU)
instruments.status: Published 10 July 2025. The Commission and the AI Board have confirmed it is an adequate voluntary tool for providers to show they comply with the AI Act. The official list names 22 signatories of all chapters (page last updated 25 November 2026). xAI signed only the Safety and Security chapter, so it must show compliance with the transparency and copyright obligations by other means. Meta declined to sign: its chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan wrote on LinkedIn on 18 July 2025 that 'Meta won't be signing it' (reported by TechCrunch).
instruments.what: A voluntary code, prepared by independent experts, that providers of general-purpose AI models can sign to show they meet their AI Act obligations. Its Transparency and Copyright chapters cover all providers; its Safety and Security chapter applies only to providers of the most advanced models, those with systemic risk.

instruments.name: AI Omnibus (amendment to the EU AI Act)
instruments.status: Proposed by the Commission on 19 November 2025. Political agreement on 7 May 2026. In force since 27 July 2026.
instruments.what: Moves the start of rules for high-risk AI systems to 2 December 2027 (uses listed in Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (AI in products listed in Annex I), and adds a ban on AI systems that generate non-consensual sexually explicit content or child sexual abuse material, applying from December 2026. It extends the AI Office's oversight to some AI systems built on general-purpose models; the Commission's announcement does not describe direct changes to the obligations for general-purpose AI models themselves.

instruments.name: California SB 53, Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act
instruments.status: Signed 29 September 2025. In force since 1 January 2026, with some provisions starting 1 January 2027. Enforced by the California Attorney General, whose office said on 24 September 2026 that 'California is actively engaged in holding frontier AI labs accountable' under the law.
instruments.what: Frontier developers (models trained with more than 10^26 operations) must publish a transparency report when they deploy a new or substantially modified model, and large frontier developers (annual revenue above $500 million) must publish a frontier AI framework, review it at least once a year, and report critical safety incidents to the California Office of Emergency Services within 15 days, or 24 hours if there is imminent risk of death or serious injury. The law protects employees who report safety risks, sets civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, and creates a consortium to design a public computing cluster called CalCompute.

instruments.name: New York RAISE Act (Responsible AI Safety and Education Act)
instruments.status: Governor Hochul signed it on 19 December 2025 on condition that the legislature pass agreed amendments (S6953B/A6453B). She signed the final version on 27 March 2026 (reported by the law firm Davis Polk). It takes effect on 1 January 2027.
instruments.what: Large frontier developers (frontier models trained with more than 10^26 operations, annual revenue above $500 million) must publish a frontier AI framework, update it every year, and report critical safety incidents to the New York Department of Financial Services within 72 hours, or 24 hours if there is imminent risk of death or serious injury. It creates an oversight office within that department, and the Attorney General can seek penalties of up to $1 million for a first violation and up to $3 million for later ones.

instruments.name: US Executive Order 14365, Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence
instruments.status: Signed 11 December 2025.
instruments.what: Directs the Attorney General to set up an AI Litigation Task Force whose sole job is to challenge state AI laws that conflict with the order's national policy, and directs the Commerce Department to publish a review of state AI laws and to limit some broadband funding for states with laws it flags. It also asks White House advisers to draft a federal framework that would preempt conflicting state AI laws, with carve-outs that include child safety protections.

instruments.name: South Korea AI Basic Act
instruments.status: In force since 22 January 2026, with its Enforcement Decree. The science ministry (MSIT) has said it will generally defer fact-finding investigations and fines for at least one year, except in cases of serious harm (as described by the US International Trade Administration, May 2026).
instruments.what: Requires providers of high-impact or generative AI to tell users in advance that AI is in use, and operators of high-impact AI to apply risk management, explainability, human oversight and record-keeping. Large AI systems trained with more than 10^26 FLOPs may face extra duties to identify, assess and manage risks, and some foreign operators must appoint a local representative.

instruments.name: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225)
instruments.jurisdiction: Council of Europe (open to non-member states)
instruments.status: Opened for signature 5 September 2024. Not yet in force: it needs ratification by 5 states, including at least 3 Council of Europe member states. As of 2026-11-26 the Netherlands treaty database lists 21 signatories and 2 ratifications: the European Union (15 May 2026) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (28 October 2026).
instruments.what: A treaty that requires parties to carry out risk and impact assessments of AI systems, give people affected by AI decisions information and a way to complain, and tell people when they are interacting with an AI system. It covers public authorities and, either directly or through other measures, private actors; national security, national defence and most research and development are excluded.

instruments.name: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (China)
instruments.status: Released 15 September 2025 at the 2025 National Cybersecurity Publicity Week. Replaces version 1.0, published in September 2024.
instruments.what: Guidance issued as a national cybersecurity standards technical document, drafted under the Cyberspace Administration of China with work led by the National Computer Network Emergency Response Technical Team/Coordination Center (CNCERT/CC) and published by the TC260 standards committee. It sets out governance principles, a classification of AI safety risks, technical measures and lifecycle safety guidelines; version 2.0 adds a category for wider societal risks such as job displacement and energy use, and grades risks into five levels by application scenario, level of intelligence and scale.

instruments.name: The Bletchley Declaration
instruments.status: Agreed by the countries attending the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, UK, on 1-2 November 2023: 28 countries and the European Union. New Zealand joined on 23 October 2024.
instruments.what: States that highly capable general-purpose AI models at the frontier could cause serious harm, through misuse or loss of human control, particularly in cybersecurity and biotechnology. Signatories agreed to cooperate on building a shared, evidence-based scientific understanding of frontier AI risks.
parties: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

instruments.name: Seoul Declaration for safe, innovative and inclusive AI
instruments.status: Agreed by participants in the leaders' session of the AI Seoul Summit on 21 May 2024. Published with an annex, the Seoul Statement of Intent toward International Cooperation on AI Safety Science.
instruments.what: Participants affirm international cooperation on AI that balances safety, innovation and inclusivity. They support creating or expanding AI safety institutes and research programmes and building networks among them to share safety research.

instruments.name: Frontier AI Safety Commitments (AI Seoul Summit 2024)
instruments.jurisdiction: International (announced by the UK and Republic of Korea governments)
instruments.status: Announced 21 May 2024 with 16 companies. Four more (Magic, Minimax, 01.ai, NVIDIA) were added on 7 February 2025, the official page's last update as of 2026-11-26.
instruments.what: Companies agreed to assess risks across the AI lifecycle, set thresholds for severe risks they would consider intolerable, and not develop or deploy a model if risks cannot be kept below those thresholds. They committed to publish a safety framework focused on severe risks by the AI summit in France (February 2025) and to report publicly on their safety approach.

instruments.name: Statement on Inclusive and Sustainable Artificial Intelligence for People and the Planet (AI Action Summit, Paris)
instruments.status: Issued 11 February 2025 after the AI Action Summit in Paris (10-11 February 2025). The official list has 63 countries plus the African Union Commission and the European Union. The United States and the United Kingdom did not sign (reported by TechCrunch, 11 February 2025).
instruments.what: Signatories commit to broaden access to AI, keep AI open, safe, secure and trustworthy, avoid market concentration, and make AI good for jobs and the environment, with stronger international cooperation on governance. It has a section on trust and safety that refers to the earlier AI safety summits.

instruments.name: New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact (AI Impact Summit 2026)
instruments.status: Adopted at the close of the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February 2026. India's public broadcaster All India Radio reported on 21 February 2026 that 88 countries and international organisations had endorsed it.
instruments.what: Calls for cooperation across the summit's seven pillars, which include trustworthiness of AI systems, human capital, energy efficiency, AI in science and economic growth. It comes with a voluntary, non-binding Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI and Voluntary Guiding Principles on Resilient, Innovative and Efficient AI.

instruments.name: New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments
instruments.jurisdiction: International (announced by the Government of India)
instruments.status: Announced 19 February 2026 by India's IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw at the AI Impact Summit (Press Trust of India report).
instruments.what: Voluntary commitments by frontier AI companies and Indian AI developers to share anonymised, aggregated insights on real-world AI use to inform policy on jobs and skills, and to strengthen multilingual and contextual evaluations of AI systems, especially for the Global South.

instruments.name: International AI summit series (Bletchley 2023 to Geneva 2027)
instruments.status: Held so far as the AI Safety Summit (Bletchley Park, UK, November 2023), the AI Seoul Summit (May 2024), the AI Action Summit (Paris, February 2025) and the AI Impact Summit (New Delhi, February 2026). Switzerland will host the fifth, the Geneva AI Summit 2027, at Palexpo in Geneva on 21-22 June 2027.
instruments.what: A recurring meeting of governments, companies and researchers on AI governance, with a new host and a new name each time. The Geneva 2027 summit's theme is 'Bridging Innovation and Trust', with two priorities: AI as a driver of prosperity, and 'trustworthy, responsible and safe use'.

instruments.name: Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework 2.0 (G7 / OECD)
instruments.status: Version 2.0 launched 28 May 2026 in Paris, on the margins of the G7 Digital and Tech Ministerial Meeting. The first version was launched in February 2025.
instruments.what: A voluntary framework in which organisations publicly report how they apply the G7 Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organisations Developing Advanced AI Systems, including risk management, risk assessment, incident reporting and information sharing. The first round produced 25 reports; more than 50 organisations pledged to report under version 2.0, which adds role-specific questions and covers agentic AI.

instruments.name: International AI Safety Report 2026
instruments.status: Published 3 February 2026. Second annual edition; the first was published 29 January 2025.
instruments.what: A review of scientific research on the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI, chaired by Yoshua Bengio and written by over 100 experts, with an Expert Advisory Panel nominated by over 30 countries and international organisations. The 2026 edition covers current and projected capabilities (with forecasts to 2030), risks from malicious use, malfunctions and systemic effects, and the limits of current risk management; the advisory panel gave technical feedback and does not endorse any policy approach.

instruments.name: International AI Safety Report Key Updates (First: Capabilities and Risk Implications; Second: Technical Safeguards and Risk Management)
instruments.status: First Key Update published 15 October 2025; Second Key Update published 25 November 2025. No later key update was listed on the publications page as of 2026-11-26.
instruments.what: Shorter updates published between the annual reports. The second covers technical safeguards, from training and deployment to post-deployment monitoring and watermarking; it finds that sophisticated attackers can often bypass current defences and that the number of companies publishing frontier AI safety frameworks more than doubled in 2025.

instruments.name: Independent International Scientific Panel on AI (United Nations)
instruments.status: Established by UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/79/325 in August 2025. The General Assembly appointed its 40 members on 12 February 2026 for a term ending 11 February 2029, by a recorded vote of 117 in favour, 2 against (Paraguay, United States) and 2 abstentions (Tunisia, Ukraine).
instruments.what: A UN body of 40 experts, co-chaired by Yoshua Bengio and Maria Ressa, that issues an annual report of evidence-based scientific assessments of AI's opportunities, risks and impacts. It released a Preliminary Report on 1 July 2026 and its first thematic brief, on AI agents and misalignment risks, on 21 September 2026. At the appointment vote the United States called the Panel and the Global Dialogue 'a significant overreach of the UN's mandate and competence'.

instruments.name: Global Dialogue on AI Governance (United Nations)
instruments.status: Established by UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/79/325 in August 2025. First session held in Geneva on 6-7 July 2026; the next is planned at UN Headquarters in New York in May 2027.
instruments.what: A forum under a General Assembly mandate where governments and other stakeholders discuss international cooperation on AI governance, exchange good practices and share information on significant AI incidents. The Scientific Panel presents its findings there; the first session was co-chaired by the UN ambassadors of El Salvador (Egriselda López) and Estonia (Rein Tammsaar).

instruments.name: The 2026 Singapore Consensus on Global AI Safety Research Priorities
instruments.status: Posted on arXiv 9 July 2026. Second edition; the first (2025) edition came out of the 2025 Singapore Conference on AI and was posted on arXiv 25 June 2025.
instruments.what: A list of technical AI safety research problems that its contributors agree are priorities, produced as an outcome of the second International Scientific Exchange on AI Safety. It draws on over 100 contributors from 13 countries, including frontier developers, government safety institutes, academia and civil society, and adds a focus on societal resilience and on risks from autonomous AI agents; the 2025 edition grouped research into Development, Assessment and Control.

instruments.name: IDAIS-London statement (International Dialogues on AI Safety)
instruments.jurisdiction: International (statement by scientists and policy experts)
instruments.status: Agreed at a dialogue held 17-19 April 2026 at the Royal Society, London, co-hosted by the Safe AI Forum and the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative. Signatories include Andrew Yao, Yoshua Bengio, Ya-Qin Zhang, Stuart Russell and Fu Ying.
instruments.what: Calls on states to treat AI-enabled cyberattack and biological misuse as a shared threat and commit to prevention. It recommends pre-deployment testing of frontier models for cyberattack capability, hardened critical infrastructure, tiered biological evaluations, pre-training data filtering for open-weight models and internationally coordinated mandatory screening of nucleic acid synthesis.

instruments.name: IDAIS-Shanghai: Consensus Statement on Ensuring Alignment and Human Control of Advanced AI Systems to Safeguard Human Flourishing
instruments.jurisdiction: International (statement by scientists and policy experts)
instruments.status: Agreed at a dialogue held 22-25 July 2025 in Shanghai, hosted by the Safe AI Forum with the Shanghai Qi Zhi Institute and Shanghai AI Laboratory. Signatories include Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Andrew Yao, Stuart Russell and Ya-Qin Zhang.
instruments.what: Calls for frontier developers to run rigorous safety evaluations, commit to third-party evaluations and present high-confidence safety cases to authorities. It also calls for globally agreed, verifiable red lines that AI systems must never cross, an international coordination body, and investment in safe-by-design research.

instruments.name: IDAIS-Venice: Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good
instruments.jurisdiction: International (statement by scientists and policy experts)
instruments.status: Agreed at a dialogue held 5-8 September 2024 in Venice, hosted by the Safe AI Forum with the Berggruen Institute.
instruments.what: Recommends emergency preparedness agreements and institutions, a safety assurance framework in which developers make a high-confidence safety case before deploying models above capability thresholds, and independent global research on verifying safety claims.

instruments.name: IDAIS-Beijing statement (red lines)
instruments.jurisdiction: International (statement by scientists and policy experts)
instruments.status: Agreed at a dialogue held 10-11 March 2024 in Beijing.
instruments.what: Proposes red lines that no AI system should cross: copying or improving itself without human approval, seeking power, substantially helping build weapons of mass destruction, autonomously executing serious cyberattacks, and deceiving its designers or regulators about these risks. It also proposes registration of advanced models above thresholds, international audits, and directing at least a third of AI research and development budgets to safety.

instruments.name: IDAIS-Oxford statement
instruments.jurisdiction: International (statement by scientists and policy experts)
instruments.status: Agreed at the first International Dialogue on AI Safety, held 31 October 2023 at Ditchley Park, UK, convened by Yoshua Bengio, Andrew Yao, Stuart Russell and Ya-Qin Zhang.
instruments.what: Calls for leading developers to spend at least one third of their AI research and development on safety, mandatory registration of models above a capability threshold, independent audits, and red lines that would require shutting down a system and all its copies if crossed.

ratings.method: A panel of seven independent AI researchers and governance experts graded nine companies A to F in six domains (37 indicators), using public materials and a company survey collected up to 3 June 2026; the overall score averages the experts' grades on a US GPA scale (A=4.0, F=0).

ratings.edition: Up to date as of July 2026
ratings.method: SaferAI staff scored each company's published frontier safety framework against 65 criteria in four equally weighted dimensions (risk identification, risk analysis and evaluation, risk treatment, risk governance); 100% would mean strong and sufficient risk management practices.

ratings.edition: Scorecard, up to date as of September 2025 (final; the site is no longer maintained)
ratings.method: Zach Stein-Perlman scored seven companies on safety actions grouped into seven weighted categories, using public information, and says the scores and weights are largely judgment calls.

ratings.edition: AI Control: An Assessment of Frontier Practices
ratings.method: Guidelight scored five companies 0 to 5 on six practices from its Control standard using only public materials (system cards, safety frameworks, risk reports, blog posts and third-party descriptions), current through 18 August 2026; the overall grade is the average of the six scores converted to a letter grade.
